claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the relative atomic diffusivities of the constituent elements during synthesis.
A narrow range of constituent diffusivity ratios promotes homogeneous alloying.
A narrow range of constituent diffusivity ratios prevents phase separation and elemental segregation.
Synthesis temperature and time can be controlled to modulate the relative atomic diffusivities of the constituent elements.
An inert or reducing atmosphere prevents oxidation during synthesis.
When constituent diffusivities are within a specific range, the elements mix uniformly before phase separation or segregation occurs.
Outside the proposed diffusivity range, slower-diffusing elements fail to integrate into the alloy.
Outside the proposed diffusivity range, faster-diffusing elements segregate.
Diffusivity mismatch leads to phase separation or uncontrolled nanoparticle morphology.
Conditions producing diffusivities within the optimal range will yield homogeneous high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles formed within the proposed optimal diffusivity range will retain substantial surface-atom exposure.
Outside the optimal diffusivity range, phase separation, elemental segregation, or uncontrolled morphology will dominate.
Failure to control or optimize atomic diffusivities leads to inconsistent or non-homogeneous nanoparticle formation.
The hypothesis applies to noble metal–based high-entropy alloy systems containing more than five elements when diffusivities can be meaningfully controlled through synthesis parameters.
The hypothesis may not apply when extreme disparities in atomic size or bonding characteristics inherently prevent alloying.
The optimal range of relative atomic diffusivities may vary among noble metal systems.
